clue.text: Possibly con lady (but not Artemis) in ancient city

indicators.note: possibly suggests these letters might be arranged another way, so the words con lady are rearranged

explanation.surface: A trickster woman, not the goddess Artemis, is at large in an old Greek town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges CONLADY. The bracket nods to the myth in which Artemis sent a boar to ravage this Greek city, hunted by the heroine Atalanta.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a city of Aetolia in Greek legend, home of King Oeneus and site of the famous boar hunt.

clue.text: Novelist truly in the van? On the contrary

indicators.note: in signals that one piece sits within another, here combined with the reversal of roles that follows
on the contrary says the containment runs the other way: the van goes inside the word for truly, not truly in the van

parts.note: certes is an archaic word meaning truly or certainly

explanation.surface: A writer asks whether something is honestly at the front of the vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks whether something is truly at the front; 'On the contrary' tells the solver to swap container and contents, so the archaic word for truly holds the van.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote, so he is a novelist.

clue.text: Word for word misprint

definitions.meaning: a word-for-word translation follows the original exactly
in printing jargon a typo involving a single letter is called by this name

explanation.definitionFit: A verbatim rendering is literal, and printers call a typographical error a literal.

clue.text: Zenith car manufacturer seen in novel circumstances

definitions.text: Zenith car manufacturer seen in novel circumstances

parts.words: Zenith car manufacturer seen in novel circumstances
parts.note: Zenith is Sinclair Lewis's fictional Midwestern city; the clue describes the title character of a 1929 Lewis novel, a retired motor magnate who travels in Europe

explanation.surface: A carmaker from the top of the range turns up in unusual situations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zenith' looks like 'peak' and 'novel' like 'new', but Zenith is Lewis's invented city and 'novel' is literal: the man appears in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Dodsworth, the Zenith automobile maker, is the hero of the Sinclair Lewis novel bearing his surname.

clue.text: Rosamond Lehmann's was in music

parts.note: Rosamond Lehmann published the 1930 novel A ___ in Music; the clue completes that title

explanation.surface: A novelist's something was set to a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a remark about Lehmann's career; it is her title A Note in Music with the key word left for the solver.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1930 Rosamond Lehmann novel is titled A Note in Music, so her item 'in music' is a musical tone.

clue.text: Attraction of Merrill's stage work

definitions.meaning: an attraction is a lure that draws something in, as food on a hook does
the American poet James Merrill wrote a play with this title

explanation.definitionFit: A lure is an enticement, and James Merrill's early verse play carries the same title.

clue.text: Plot airmen reworked for verse by John Pudney, RAF

indicators.note: reworked means the letters of plot airmen are made over into a new order

explanation.surface: An RAF poet's scheme involving flyers is revised into a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reworked' rearranges PLOTAIRMEN. John Pudney was a Second World War RAF officer and poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Pudney, the wartime RAF poet, wrote a poem with this springboard as its title.

clue.text: Support for artist from oriental sort of sale

parts.note: E stands for east, so oriental gives that compass letter

indicators.note: sort of says the word sale appears only in a kind of version, its letters reshuffled

explanation.surface: Something for a painter comes from an Eastern bazaar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges the four letters of 'sale', which follow the compass letter for east.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter rests the canvas on this wooden stand while working.

clue.text: The Spanish in a row in studio

indicators.note: in places the Spanish article within the word for a row

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
el is the Spanish word for the

explanation.surface: Spaniards are seated in a line inside a workshop.
explanation.definitionFit: This French word for an artist's or designer's workroom is used in English too.

clue.text: He alone concludes gothic trilogy

parts.note: Mervyn Peake's Gormenghast trilogy ends with a volume named after its hero followed by the word Alone

explanation.surface: A solitary man brings a dark trilogy to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He alone' sounds like a description of a lonely hero; it is the shape of Peake's third title, '___ Alone'.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus Alone is the final book of Peake's Gormenghast series, whose hero is Titus Groan.

clue.text: Valued, like O'Brian's ships

definitions.meaning: Patrick O'Brian's naval novels describe Royal Navy warships classed as first- to sixth-rates by their guns

explanation.definitionFit: Something assessed is graded, and Nelson-era warships were graded by class in Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey novels.

clue.text: Cut page for Shakespearian doll

definitions.meaning: a page cut or torn from a publication, as an advertiser's proof
Doll is the prostitute in Henry IV Part 2, whose surname completes the phrase

explanation.definitionFit: A page torn out as proof is a tear sheet, and Doll Tearsheet is Falstaff's companion in Henry IV Part 2.

clue.text: "… those — fly / Of sad distrust and jealousy" (Edmund Waller)

definitions.text: … those — fly / Of sad distrust and jealousy" (Edmund Waller)

parts.words: … those — fly / Of sad distrust and jealousy" (Edmund Waller)
parts.note: a quotation from Waller with a missing word: the missing plural is something shot that flies through the air

explanation.surface: A line of Waller's verse with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill-in quotation clues give the line with a dash; the missing word fits the metaphor of things that fly and wound.
explanation.definitionFit: Waller's line pictures distrust and jealousy as missiles shot from a bow.

clue.text: Early novelist who introduced profound changes

definitions.text: Early novelist who introduced profound changes

parts.words: Early novelist who introduced profound changes
parts.note: the Roman author whose Metamorphoses, or The Golden Ass, is among the first novels; metamorphoses are profound changes

explanation.surface: A pioneering writer brought in sweeping reforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introduced profound changes' sounds like a reformer; it describes a book called Metamorphoses.
explanation.definitionFit: Apuleius wrote the second-century Latin novel Metamorphoses, often called The Golden Ass.

clue.text: A teacher of Rabelais and Shakespeare

definitions.text: A teacher of Rabelais and Shakespeare

parts.words: A teacher of Rabelais and Shakespeare
parts.note: one name belongs both to Gargantua's sophist tutor in Rabelais and to the pedantic schoolmaster in Love's Labour's Lost

explanation.surface: Someone taught both a French satirist and the Bard.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue seems to say someone taught the two writers; 'of' means a teacher appearing in their works.
explanation.definitionFit: Holofernes is Gargantua's tutor in Rabelais and the schoolmaster in Love's Labour's Lost.

clue.text: Anne, who offered her earthly possessions in 1977 — later a saint maybe IS Aran Islander nominally gets returned mail

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held runs into 15-across's clue ('Anne, who offered her earthly possessions in 1977 — later a saint maybe IS Aran Islander nominally gets returned mail') with no count; no scan to restore the printed clue.
annotationWithheld.clue: Anne, who offered her earthly possessions in 1977 — later a saint maybe IS Aran Islander nominally gets returned mail

clue.text: Aran Islander nominally gets returned mail

definitions.text: Aran Islander nominally gets returned mail

parts.words: Aran Islander nominally gets returned mail
parts.note: a writer born on the Aran Islands whose first name, Liam, is the word mail read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone living off the west of Ireland has letters sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nominally' says the reversed 'mail' is about his name: LIAM, as in Liam O'Flaherty, novelist born on Inishmore in the Aran Islands off western Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Liam O'Flaherty was born on Inishmore in the Aran Islands.

clue.text: Name of section (as for Lear, or Bleak)

definitions.text: Name of section (as for Lear, or Bleak)

parts.words: Name of section (as for Lear, or Bleak)
parts.note: Lear is part of King Lear and Bleak part of Bleak House: each is a portion of a book's name, and in printing this term is the page bearing only a short form of the book's name

explanation.surface: A heading for part of a book, illustrated with two famous works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name of section' suggests a chapter heading; the examples show half of a title, and in bookmaking a half-title is the page with just the short name before the title page.
explanation.definitionFit: In books, the half-title is the leaf before the title page bearing the shortened name; Lear and Bleak are halves of full names.

clue.text: Hofmannsthal wrote this 24 hours ago?

definitions.meaning: Hugo von Hofmannsthal's early verse play Gestern has this English title
twenty-four hours ago means the day before today

explanation.definitionFit: Hofmannsthal's 1891 play Gestern translates as the day before today.

clue.text: Incomplete Marjorie Rawlings title (for remainder, see under)

definitions.text: Incomplete Marjorie Rawlings title (for remainder, see under)

parts.words: Incomplete Marjorie Rawlings title (for remainder, see under)
parts.note: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings wrote a 1933 novel whose title ends with the word Under; the clue gives the rest

explanation.surface: A partial book title, with a pointer to find the missing part below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see under' looks like a cross-reference note; it is literal, the missing last word of the title being Under.
explanation.definitionFit: Rawlings's first novel is South Moon Under, so these two words are the title minus its last word.

clue.text: Joyce made him bloom, say

parts.note: James Joyce recast the Homeric hero as Leopold Bloom in his 1922 novel

explanation.surface: Joyce caused a man to flower, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloom' looks like flowering; it is Leopold Bloom, Joyce's modern version of Homer's hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's novel Ulysses makes Leopold Bloom its modern counterpart of Odysseus, whose Latin name this is.

clue.text: Disgraceful louts joining consumers of Homer

indicators.note: disgraceful suggests something unseemly is done to the word louts, here a rearrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: Badly behaved yobs join Homer's eaters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disgraceful' rearranges LOUTS. The definition is cryptic: this word joined to 'eaters' names the consumers in Homer's Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Odyssey the Lotus-eaters are a people who eat a fruit that makes men forget home.

clue.text: Height of Brooke's poetic art

definitions.meaning: a height is a raised area of land, a rise
Rupert Brooke wrote a sonnet with this title

explanation.definitionFit: A rise of ground can be called the hill, and The Hill is a love sonnet by Rupert Brooke.

clue.text: Coward's work, something to be sneezed at

definitions.meaning: Noel Coward wrote a 1925 comedy with this title
a pollen allergy whose symptom is sneezing

explanation.definitionFit: Coward's comedy of manners has this name, and the pollen allergy makes sufferers sneeze.

clue.text: Earthmoving short-story writer

indicators.note: moving says the letters of earth are shifted about into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A writer of short fiction digs up the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges EARTH; the clue joins the two words into 'Earthmoving' to disguise the split.
explanation.definitionFit: Bret Harte was an American writer known for stories of the California gold rush.

clue.text: Murdered king a very fat man according to some judges

definitions.text: Murdered king a very fat man according to some judges

parts.words: Murdered king a very fat man according to some judges
parts.note: the Book of Judges tells of a very fat Moabite king stabbed by Ehud

explanation.surface: A slain ruler was obese, in some critics' opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'according to some judges' sounds like a matter of opinion; it means the biblical Book of Judges.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglon, king of Moab, was a very fat man killed by Ehud in Judges 3.

clue.text: Essayist in chaste electorate

indicators.note: in shows the essayist's name sits within the phrase chaste electorate, across the word break

explanation.surface: A writer is found among a virtuous body of voters.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'chaste' into 'electorate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Steele co-founded The Tatler and The Spectator and was a leading 18th-century essayist.

clue.text: God indicating some prize used to be more attainable

indicators.note: some means only part of the phrase prize used is taken, a run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: A deity shows that a trophy was once easier to win.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle 'prize' and 'used'; 'indicating' and the rest of the clue are surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeus is the chief of the Greek gods.

clue.text: Euphues' golden legacy

parts.note: Thomas Lodge's 1590 prose romance carries the subtitle Euphues' Golden Legacy, after Lyly's character

explanation.surface: A character's precious bequest.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue looks like a reference to an inheritance; it is the subtitle of Lodge's romance, the source of As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: Lodge's romance, subtitled Euphues' Golden Legacy, is named for its heroine, Shakespeare's model for Rosalind.

clue.text: Group of stanzas in different metres suggested by secret society

definitions.text: Group of stanzas in different metres
definitions.meaning: in a Pindaric ode, strophe, antistrophe and epode form a set of three

explanation.definitionFit: The three-part strophe, antistrophe and epode unit is so named, as are Chinese criminal gangs.

clue.text: Their library was potted at Qumran

definitions.text: Their library was potted at Qumran

parts.words: Their library was potted at Qumran
parts.note: the Dead Sea Scrolls, found in clay jars in caves at Qumran, are linked to a Jewish ascetic sect

explanation.surface: A group's books were abridged at an archaeological site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potted' suggests summarised, as in a potted history; here the scrolls were literally stored in pots.
explanation.definitionFit: The Essenes, a Jewish sect, are traditionally credited with the Dead Sea Scrolls found in jars at Qumran.

clue.text: "Eton Atheist" — yes, he'll reform

indicators.note: reform means the letters of yes and he'll are shaped anew, as a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A schoolboy unbeliever agrees he will mend his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges YESHELL. The poet was nicknamed the Eton Atheist for his schoolboy irreligion.
explanation.definitionFit: Percy Bysshe Shelley was known at Eton as 'the Atheist' and later expelled from Oxford for atheism.
